title: Tissue Healing, Muscle Injury and Load Management Principles
lead: The biology that guides every rehabilitation timeline in this volume.

rows: Approximate timing (varies by tissue and injury)
Bleeding, swelling, inflammatory cells clear debris
Protect, control swelling, gentle movement as allowed
New collagen and blood vessels form; tissue is weak and disorganised
Progressive, controlled loading to guide repair
Collagen reorganises along lines of stress, tissue strengthens
Progressive heavy and specific loading, return to function

blocks.text: Healing speed differs: muscle (good blood supply) heals faster than tendon, ligament and cartilage.

sections.title: 12.2 Acute soft-tissue injury: PEACE and LOVE

blocks.text: A widely taught framework [Ref – to verify Dubois and Esculier 2020]:

items: **Immediately (PEACE)**: **P**rotect (relative rest for a few days), **E**levate, **A**void anti-inflammatories and ice early (possible interference with healing; debated), **C**ompress, **E**ducate.
**After the first days (LOVE)**: **L**oad (let pain guide progression), **O**ptimism, **V**ascularisation (pain-free aerobic exercise), **E**xercise.

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: The older RICE message focused on rest. Current thinking favours early, optimal loading because tissues remodel in response to load.

blocks.text: Muscle strains are most common in two-joint muscles that work eccentrically at high speed: hamstrings, rectus femoris, adductors, gastrocnemius. Classification systems (for example the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification, BAMIC) grade injuries by MRI extent and site, including whether the tendon is involved; intramuscular tendon injuries may need longer rehabilitation [Ref – to verify].

rows: Pain with stretch and contraction, minimal strength loss
Clear strength loss, limited range, bruising possible
Complete or near-complete tear, palpable gap, major loss of function; surgical opinion for some (for example proximal hamstring avulsion)

items: **Protection** (days): reduce bleeding and pain; isometric contractions within comfort; walking as able.
**Restore range and strength**: progressive isotonic loading, increasing length.
**Eccentric and long-length strength**: for example Nordic hamstring exercise for hamstrings.
**Running progression**: from jogging to high speed; acceleration and deceleration.
**Sport-specific**: change of direction, kicking, full training.

blocks.text: Injuries often happen when load rises faster than tissue capacity. Monitor training volume and intensity. Large, sudden spikes in load compared with what an athlete is used to are linked with higher injury risk [Ref – to verify; the acute:chronic workload ratio model is debated]. Practical rule: progress gradually and plan recovery.
For tendon and many overuse conditions, a common approach is:

items: Pain during exercise up to about 3 to 5 out of 10 is acceptable.
Pain should settle within 24 hours and not increase the next morning.
If it does, reduce load next session.
**Why do tendons take longer to heal than muscle?** Poorer blood supply and slower collagen turnover.
**What does LOVE stand for?** Load, Optimism, Vascularisation, Exercise.
**Which muscles are most often strained?** Two-joint muscles working eccentrically at high speed.
**Why progress loading during remodelling?** Collagen aligns and strengthens in response to load.
**What does the pain-monitoring model allow?** Training with acceptable pain while avoiding next-day flares.
